Since the remains of at least 1505 children were found at the sites of former residential schools, voices have been rising to cancel Canada Day. Thousands of Indigenous and non-Indigenous people are marching through the streets of Montréal in solidarity with residential school victims and survivors. The colour of this July 1 is not white or red, but orange.
L’atmosphère, lourde de deuil et de colè: The atmosphere, heavy with grief and anger, is nothing like the usual July 1 festivities. “Why are we wearing orange today? We are lighting the sacred fire that is in each of us,” says Kevin Deer, spiritual leader of Kahnawake, in his opening address.

It would give us an immense reprieve!” Many of the Indigenous people present are tired of always having to put their demands forward again.

Tu es une survivante de troisième généra: You’re a third-generation residential school survivor. Your father is Indigenous, and your mother is Punjabi. How were these subjects addressed in your family?
Ma famille a des traumatismes intergénér: My family has intergenerational trauma. My father isn’t able to have these conversations. He has a lot of identity issues and spiritual confusion because of his experiences in day schools and Catholic churches. I would have liked to have detailed conversations with him. He has his own mental health struggles. I respect him and I love him immensely.
Mon grand-père est allé à la guerre pour: My grandfather went to war to defend Canada. My great-grandparents met in the residential schools, and they became enfranchised in order to become Canadian citizens. They had to give up everything: their Indigenous status, their land, their rights to the land. They could no longer go back home to the reserve. I want to educate people about enfranchisement issues, like the one my family went through.
Ma grand-mère était mon seul vrai lien à: My grandmother was my only real link to our family line, before she passed away several years ago. By speaking today, I really wanted to honour my father, my grandmother and everyone who helped me reconnect with my identity. I spoke about my experiences of abuse by white non-Indigenous people who want to control our space and play the saviour. And that’s unacceptable, because it has a lasting impact. My mother didn’t approach these subjects in the most sensitive way; she never really understood our struggles.
She has her own identity issues. She was born in Kuwait, far from her home country, and she had to overcome prejudice against Punjabi women to become a lawyer. Like her, I internalized the desire to be white. But as I grew up, I realized it didn’t work.
<strong>Tu as dit dans ton témoignage au: You said in your testimony today that this is the first time in seven years that you feel fully Indigenous. What happened during that time?
Je me sentais pleinement autochtone à l’: I felt fully Indigenous back when I went to an Indigenous school. I was learning my culture and my language every day. I drummed and I sang. Even though I was bullied, I felt that these people were my family. I left my Indigenous school and thought I was the bad guy, the traitor. It affected me for years. I hated being Indigenous for a long time. I had a deep hatred for the person I was when I was younger. I didn’t sing or dance for six years.
Maintenant que je suis plus vieille, je: Now that I’m older, I understand that I’m proudly Indigenous and that no non-Indigenous person can decide how much love I have for my culture. The mentality of good Indigenous people and bad Indigenous people comes from colonization. It was used in the residential schools and in the Sixties Scoop. Indigenous people were divided by this colonial binary. It’s so hard to feel that my way of life isn’t colonial. The Ojibwe language isn’t even on Google Translate! There are no Indigenous languages on Google, so it’s really hard for me to reconnect with my culture without a community. It’s a deep wound. But in Montréal, I’ve found a great diversity of Indigenous people – Inuit, Cree, Algonquin, Mohawk. I really hope this will give me a second chance to reconnect with my culture, because I deserve it. My family line deserves to heal.
Enfant, j’ai été victime d’abus aux main: As a child, I was abused by a white teacher who tried to infiltrate our community. My abuser was a white British teacher who had joined the school 20 years earlier and stayed. The community adopted him, and he had an enormous influence on very young students. He hindered our efforts to revitalize and reconnect with our culture. He thought he could contribute with his British military ways, but that wasn’t what we needed.
Mon agresseur a utilisé ma culture contr: My abuser used my culture against me and used our teachings against me. He accused me of lying and told me I was a threat to society because I didn’t want to conform. I was a traumatized child, I had problems at home and I was very sensitive. He exploited those traits against me. If I made a mistake, he took it very personally. This man spoke the language, he led the drum groups for boys. He had a big role in ceremonies, he held the sacred feathers, he spoke about our cultural teachings. I understand that we sometimes adopt people into our communities and that we can be desperate for allies, but we have to scrupulously examine the non-Indigenous people who join us. There should be background checks in schools. For years, I thought I was the only one. When I heard the testimonies of my abuser’s current students, I cried. I hope there will be justice.
Il est entré dans la communauté à un mom: He came into the community at a time when it was very vulnerable. Unfortunately, his influence harmed a lot of people. The people who bullied me were very close to him. I can’t even blame them. His influence on them was harmful and profound. His misogyny and his other ways of thinking were so horrible. My abuser asked a lot of people to avoid me. He turned his students against me. I hope they’ll be able to begin their own healing now that he has been exposed.
Comment est-ce que renouer avec la commu: How has reconnecting with the Indigenous community in Montréal been beneficial for you?
Ça a été très thérapeutique. Dans mon té: It’s been very therapeutic. In my testimony, I talked a lot about how I feel like a guest in my own home when I drum, sing, dance, shout and speak my language. It’s my childhood fear, with its feelings of guilt and shame, telling me I don’t deserve it, that I’m a bad Indigenous person. It’s very therapeutic to see that even after all these years, there are Indigenous people who know my story and still welcome me with open arms.
Être capable de danser dans mes habits t: Being able to dance in my traditional clothing, to drum, to sing made me feel that the bond that was broken many years ago is being rebuilt. There was so much unconditional love and support today. I was moved to see thousands of people gather, because our lives are still at risk. Even though I’ve had negative experiences in Montréal, moving here gave me a new perspective. It woke me up to all the internalized hatred and fear I carried inside me.
J’ai appris aujourd’hui que je pouvais u: Today I learned that I can use my voice to bring about positive change and fight my inner demons.
Qu’est-ce que tu as fait pour prendre so: What have you done to take care of yourself and heal since the news about the residential schools came out?

It was very hard. I got word that my abuser was being investigated, and it took a huge weight off me. Recently, I started a new job with Squash Canada. On vise à promouvoir le sport et le bien: We aim to promote sport and well-being among these populations. I love this sport, I love the community that plays it, even though it has its problems. Part of my job is to research reserves across Canada and determine how far they are from sports fields and gyms. Several communities are very remote and suffer from major funding and awareness problems. I wouldn’t have accepted this position if my colleagues weren’t determined to educate themselves. I had to have discussions with them because there were things they didn’t grasp.
Bien que j’aurais aimé occuper un emploi: Although I would have liked to have a job in the Indigenous community, that hasn’t been possible. My current job as a diversity and inclusion ambassador is a chance for me to show non-Indigenous people that these issues really matter. This isn’t about opinions; it’s about history and the situation we’re facing right now. If they want me to work for them, they have to let me stand up for these issues.
Je participe à beaucoup d’événements. J’: I take part in a lot of events. I recently took part in some against the Trans Mountain pipeline. I’m an activist with the McGill Indigenous Student Alliance, Climate Justice McGill and my own racial justice group. This summer, I plan to continue my job, my activism and my volunteering.
Durant l’année scolaire, je remets en qu: During the school year, I challenge university policies. Right now, the places where I have the most opportunity to change things are the worlds of education and sport.
Comment prévois-tu utiliser ta place dan: How do you plan to use your place in the education system and the world of sport to heal the Indigenous community you’re part of?
J’ai grandi entre deux cultures. D’une p: I grew up between two cultures. On one hand, I went to an Indigenous school that emphasized revitalization, traditions, cultural ceremonies and land reclamation. On the other, I grew up in a colonial, modern world. I’ve spent my life finding the balance between the two and holding them accountable when they make mistakes. There’s a lot of division in communities and internalized colonialism because of trauma. I feel it in the education system.
Là où les deux mondes se rencontrent, il: Where the two worlds meet, there is universal knowledge. There’s a big bias in favour of European knowledge. And even though I love learning and I speak English, Indigenous people were excluded from that knowledge for a long time. I remember taking a course on genocides in high school, and I asked the teacher why the genocide of Indigenous peoples wasn’t being taught.
On a parlé de l’Holocauste, du génocide: We talked about the Holocaust, the Armenian genocide, the Rwandan genocide, but not the Indigenous genocide. I hope the children found today wake people up to the fact that the extermination of Indigenous peoples was deliberate. The education system was used against us.
On a vraiment besoin de reconstruire not: We really need to rebuild our education system, because education is for everyone and needs to be diverse.
Quelles sont les solutions à cet héritag: What are the solutions to this legacy of colonization against Indigenous peoples, and how do you see yourself moving forward?
Le mouvement Land Back est répandu à tra: The Land Back movement is widespread across the country. Even though many think we’re just going to take everything, that’s not really the goal. It’s rather a movement in which we assert the place we have always had here. Non-Indigenous people need to understand that loving Canada as a country hurts us. This country has problems of genocide, colonization, racism, white supremacy and patriarchy that we have to resolve.
Je pense que la Commission de vérité et: I think the Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada and the Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women movement are essential. We need to talk about them in work meetings. We need mandatory anti-racism modules for all students. All Canadians need to read the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s report and donate to the Indian Residential School Survivors Society to give us visibility.
Beaucoup d’autochtones se sentent aliéné: Many Indigenous people feel alienated. We don’t know where our place is in society. We have no sovereignty. We don’t control our own representation in the media and in the education system. Our stories are ignored in North America.
Nous avons besoin d’être recentrés et d’: We need to be recentred and be at the decision-making table in the House of Commons, in Parliament, on school boards. We need to be front and centre in these institutions, not just consulted. Because that’s how the treaties and the residential schools were created – with lies, deception, disrespect, lack of consultation and language barriers. This power imbalance isn’t an opinion, because there is too much evidence. We are owed reparations, and the only way they can be made is by holding the institutions of our society accountable.
On doit démonter les systèmes racistes d: We have to dismantle the racist systems in education, sport and business. My story – changing schools, being a third-generation residential school survivor, feeling lost – is proof that these systems do harm.
